# Inti: the stories first, then the spelling

You cannot weigh an accent without knowing what it carries. Here is what **Inti** has been carrying.

## The Stories That Carry the Name

**Inti, Child of the Creator.** In the theology the Inca taught at Cuzco, Inti was not the first power.  The creator Viracocha — the incomprehensible god behind the world, as the chroniclers struggled to render him — made the sun, the moon, and the stars and set them in heaven as lights for humankind.  Inti and his sister-wife Mama Quilla were thus the children of the highest god, commissioned to govern the sky in their father's place (Sarmiento de Gamboa, Historia Indica 7; Betanzos, Suma y Narración 2).

**The Golden Staff of Manco Cápac.** The founding myth of Cuzco is a solar errand.  Inti and Mama Quilla, grieving that humankind lived without law, cloth, or maize, sent their children — a son, Manco Cápac, and a daughter, Mama Ocllo — from the Island of the Sun in Lake Titicaca, bearing a golden staff.  Wherever the staff sank whole into the earth, there they were to raise the city.

**The Vision at Susurpuquio.** Before he was Pachacuti — 'He Who Shakes the Earth' — the prince Yupanqui was an unlikely heir, and the Chanka confederation stood ready to erase Cuzco.  In the account Sarmiento de Gamboa drew from Inca informants (Historia Indica 35–38), the young man took refuge at the spring of Susurpuquio, and there the Creator Viracocha came to him in a dream, and Inti promised that the sun himself would fight beside him.  The Chanka attack failed; Yupanqui became the ninth Sapa Inca; and he answered the vision on an imperial scale.

## The Name Travels

The conquest did not end Inti; it translated him.  Spanish missionaries deliberately identified the sun with the Christian God, and the great church of Santo Domingo was planted directly on the Coricancha's foundations, its colonial vaults rising around the curved Inca walls that still hold them up.
